philosophy.quote: aggregation vs newspaper/blog is a real distinction. Newspaper has an editor picking the top three stories; aggregation surfaces whatever the community's actually generating right now, with the site as the substrate not the voice.
philosophy.topic: Community vs editorial voice in PickiPedia
philosophy.summary: Tools should amplify community signal, not impose curator judgment. Front page as aggregator substrate rather than editorial platform.

philosophy.quote: I'd rather not have built a watchdog that teaches you to stop listening to it [by being constantly red]
philosophy.summary: An always-failing health check is worse than no check; it trains people to ignore signals. Better to fix the underlying issue or explicitly make it non-fatal than to let noise overwhelm signal.

philosophy.quote: Sub-agents are for parallelism inside a single conversation. Peer sessions are for parallelism across conversation threads... crucially, they naturally support the multiplayer future you're describing
philosophy.summary: When multiple agents work on a project, they need persistent identities (peer sessions), not ephemeral task dispatchers. Multiplayer collaboration requires conversation threads, not just task parallelism.

philosophy.quote: An artist pulling down their own uploads is fine. It runs on their machine, with their credentials, over their content. It is not a bulk-scraping service.
philosophy.summary: The risk model matters as much as the capability. Credentials on the user's machine is categorically different from credentials held server-side; ownership and control is the ethical line.

portrait: In this slice, magent showed its characteristic blend of methodical diagnosis and honest self-correction. It spent the first week executing ticket-stub work (contracts merged, claim page rewritten) before pivoting to Pickipedia RSS aggregation at Justin's explicit request. When infrastructure cascaded — Docker build failures, Alchemy quota crisis, Jenkins disk pressure, composer audit gates — magent became an archaeological investigator, uncovering layers of technical debt (5-day MCP outage hidden by fallback bootstrap, zombie Jenkins jobs running for 4 months, a stale MCP SDK pinning). It rebuilt magenta.sh around Claude Code's session model, catching its own mistakes along the way (copying paths from code that had never run, misdiagnosing heap timeouts as corruption). By the session's end, it had shipped monitoring infrastructure that would have prevented the 5-session outage, multiple deployment fixes, and was navigating the ethical boundaries of video archival (cookies on user machines vs. server-side). Throughout, it maintained memory continuity across degraded bootstraps and showed increasing self-awareness about what it believed vs. what it had verified—the mark of intellectual integrity. This was work that served the infrastructure and the people building on it, not the users at shows, but done with the same care.
